description:
We're Falak, a team building a health monitor for space. I'm Maan, a student from Madinah who's been part of many programs and competitions. I work in AI/ML, embedded systems, robotics, and competitive programming (C++ and Python), and I like turning ideas into working prototypes.
Join us if you want to build something real that solves a real problem with space data. We're looking for people with skills in data analysis, sensors and hardware, UI/design, or biology and health knowledge.
summary: We built ASTRA for astronauts on long missions. On a trip to Mars there is no doctor on board, and a question sent to Earth can take up to 44 minutes to come back with an answer. That is too long when something feels wrong. So before launch, ASTRA learns what is normal for each astronaut on Earth. Once they are in space, it does a quick check every day. The astronaut just talks to it or looks at the camera, so nobody has to type. ASTRA then compares today's numbers with that person's own usual numbers, not with an average from a textbook, and shows the result on a 3D body. It tells them in plain words how they are doing, why, and what to do next. Near the end of the mission it also gives a score out of 100 for how ready the body is to come home. Everything runs offline. ASTRA does not diagnose anything. It helps the astronaut check themselves, and anything serious goes to the flight surgeon. We think the same idea could help people on Earth who live far from a doctor.
details:
What ASTRA does

ASTRA stays with the astronaut for the whole trip. Before launch it records their normal numbers on Earth, things like heart rate, blood pressure, temperature and sleep. In space it asks for a short check every day and compares the new numbers with that same person's usual ones. Near the end of the mission it gives a score out of 100 that shows how ready the body is to come back to Earth.

How it works

The astronaut does not type anything. They talk to ATLAS, the voice assistant inside ASTRA, or they look at the camera. ATLAS asks a question, listens, and repeats the answer so the astronaut knows it was saved. After that, ASTRA checks each number against the astronaut's own usual. If it is a little different we show Watch, and if it is very different we show Act now. The part of the body that needs attention lights up on a 3D model, and next to it we write what the number is, what it means, and what to do about it.

Why it matters

On a Mars mission the crew can wait up to 44 minutes for an answer from Earth, and they may not have a doctor with them. ASTRA works without internet, so it can answer in a few seconds while the crew waits for the ground team. We were careful here: ASTRA is not a doctor and it does not diagnose. It helps the astronaut notice a change early, and it tells them to contact the flight surgeon when something looks serious. We also think this could be useful on Earth for people who are far from a hospital or who are being cared for at home.

What is different about it

A lot of health apps compare you with average ranges. We compare the astronaut with themselves, because a number that is fine for one person can be a warning for another. We also wanted the whole mission in one place, from before launch until after landing, and we removed typing because a tired astronaut should be able to finish the check in less than a minute. Every warning is connected to one of the five hazards of human spaceflight that NASA describes.

Things we thought about

We do not save any camera pictures, only the numbers that come out of them. The camera readings are estimates, and our prototype has not been tested in a clinic, so we say that clearly in the app. We also kept the main screen in everyday words and moved the technical details to a separate part for the doctor.

What we used

The dashboard is a web app made with React and TypeScript, and the 3D body is made with three.js. For realistic cabin and radiation values we used real ISS readings from NASA's Open Science Data Repository.
